# The Scale Transect {#sec-transect}

Scale is the first of the six [design levers](design-levers.qmd): how much ground the project takes. It is also the one most often mistaken for a fact about a site rather than a decision somebody made. Someone chose five megawatts over eighty, usually early and on grounds of interconnection and capital, and that choice rations every lever left to the design: how much ground there is to choose among, what hardware is affordable, who manages the vegetation, and who ends up owning the asset.

Scale earns a chapter because its consequences travel together. Interconnection posture, the decision unit, the permitting path, [ground-layer](terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer) management, and [siting latitude](#sec-siting-latitude) all shift as projects get bigger, and they shift closely enough that naming a position on the gradient tells you many things at once. That gradient is the **scale transect**, and A0 through A5 are named points along it rather than a separate kind of thing. What follows sets out why it is a gradient rather than a set of bins, what the zones are, how the instrument of restoration changes along the way, and why the middle of the transect behaves unlike either end.

![**The five zones.** Calibration points on the gradient rather than boxes with walls: named places to stand, so that a project near a boundary can be read as being near a boundary. Capacity is how a project is filed and acreage is how a place experiences it, so where the two disagree the acres are the better guide. Building-mounted arrays are **A0** and take no ground at all, which puts them at the origin of the gradient rather than on it.](../figures/fig_scale_transect.svg){#fig-scale-transect}

## Five zones on one gradient {#sec-zones}

A 30-kilowatt barn array and a 300-megawatt regional project are both solar on farmland, but their decision-makers, finance, grid connection, ground management, and possible land functions differ. **Scale** is therefore a transect: a gradient of attributes that change together, rather than a set of capacity bins. Capacity is a useful hint, not the definition. The zones below are calibration points on that gradient in the sense the rural-to-urban transect uses them, which is to say named places to stand rather than boxes with walls. [Pressures](terminology.qmd#term-design-pressures) shift continuously along it, a 4 MW project and a 6 MW project differ by less than their labels suggest, and a project near a boundary should be read as being near a boundary. What moves together is:

- **How it connects to the grid**: behind the meter → distribution → transmission
- **Who decides**: one landowner → several parties at a table → a utility with a place in the interconnection queue
- **What it takes to permit**: allowed by right → site plan review → full environmental review
- **Who manages the ground**: existing farm labor → purpose-built for the site → an outside contractor
- **Where the money comes from**: the owner's pocket → tax equity and a power contract → project finance
- **Who has to be talked to**: the neighbors → the township → a regional process
- **[Siting latitude](#sec-siting-latitude)**: opportunistic → strategic → decided by what land could be assembled near a substation

Physical effects change with geometry and scale as well. Soil cooling and moisture retention are more consistent than air-temperature effects, which vary by site [@zhang2025].

::: {.zone-table}
| Zone | Indicative capacity | Indicative footprint | Interconnection | Decision unit | Ground-layer management |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A1 — Farmstead** | <100 kW | under ~1 acre | Behind-the-meter, net metered | Single owner-operator | Existing farm labor and equipment |
| **A2 — Field** | 100 kW–1 MW | ~0.5–8 acres | Behind-meter to distribution | Landowner, possibly one lease counterparty | Existing equipment, modest adaptation |
| **A3 — Parcel** | 1–5 MW | ~6–30 acres | Distribution; community solar, mid-market PPA | Multi-party: landowner, developer, offtaker, tax equity | Purpose-built: dedicated mowing, contract grazing, seeded establishment |
| **A4 — Landscape** | 5–50 MW | ~30–300 acres | Distribution to sub-transmission; queue position matters | Developer-led, institutional capital | Contract enterprise: commercial graziers, habitat contracts |
| **A5 — Regional** | 50 MW+ | ~300 acres to 10,000+ | Transmission; merchant or utility PPA | Utility/IPP, multi-jurisdiction | Contract enterprise at ranch scale; multi-site rotation logistics |
:::

Capacity is how a project is filed; acreage is how landholders and communities experience it. [Trackers](terminology.qmd#term-tracking-curtailment) and [agrivoltaic](terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) clearance use more land per megawatt than dense arrays, so **acreage is the better guide when the two disagree** [@gallaher2026; @sturchio2025croplands].

**The conversion behind the acreage column, and its shelf life.** The [footprints](terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) above assume 5.5 acres per MW-AC for fixed tilt and 6.3 for single-axis tracking, which is what Berkeley Lab measures for operating systems under 20 MW; counting setbacks, access, and interconnection the total site runs nearer 6 to 8. Wide-row agrivoltaic layouts roughly double it. These are 2020s numbers and they have been falling for a decade as modules improve, so treat the acres as a conversion to redo rather than a constant, and expect a later edition of this table to show smaller footprints for the same megawatts. The fall is bounded, though. A commercial silicon module converts a little over a fifth of the light reaching it against a single-junction thermodynamic ceiling near a third, so there is roughly a third of improvement left in that architecture before physics closes it. Tandem cells can pass that ceiling, which makes the floor soft rather than fixed, but not open-ended. Land intensity will improve and then stop improving.

Building-mounted arrays are **A0**: no ground to choose, manage, share, or spare. A5 has no ceiling; its common condition is placement fixed by land assembly and restoration carried by management (§-@sec-open-issues, issue 1).

**A4 spans a wide range and probably contains a break of its own, near 20 to 25 MW.** That is not a land threshold but a jurisdictional one: it is roughly where several states move siting authority from local boards to a state office, New York's being the clearest case. Below it a township still decides, and a design argument can be made to people who live there. Above it the venue changes and so does the audience. The lexicon has not split A4 on that line yet, because unlike the 5 MW boundary it rests on one attribute rather than several converging ones, but a reader working between 20 and 25 MW should expect the project to behave like the zone above rather than the zone below (§-@sec-open-issues, issue 1).

The bands in the table fit the US Midwest and should be redrawn elsewhere. Not every zone exists in every region.

:::: {#sec-grazing .example}
**A worked example: grazing across the transect.** Sheep grazing keeps the same name from the farmstead to the region, and stops being the same job about twice along the way. Following one practice across the zones shows what the transect is actually measuring, because nothing about the animal changes and almost everything about the arrangement does.

The choice of animal is made before the scale question arises. Sheep fit standard racking, goats climb it and chew wiring, and cattle and horses need more clearance than a standard array leaves them [@merheb2025], so in practice it is sheep or it is mowing.

| Zone | Who grazes | Typical figures | The design problem |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **A1–A2** | the farm's own flock | ~3 ewes/acre in New York and Michigan experience [@hartman2026]; 4–20 sheep/acre in rotational trials at Cornell | matching stocking to the forage and the weather in front of you, rather than to a published rate |
| **A3** | a contracted grazier | ~$300–500/acre/yr for vegetation management | building a site that works for someone who does not live on it and visits on a schedule |
| **A4–A5** | a logistics enterprise | mowing medians across 54 utility-scale sites: $113/acre/yr at sheep-grazed sites, $121 at native-vegetation, $203 at turfgrass; herbicide $293 on gravel [@mccall2023] | water, gates, hauling, and rotating a flock between parcels that do not touch each other |

: Solar grazing across the transect. {#tbl-grazing}

Two terms come apart here and are worth keeping apart. **Stocking density** is how many animals are on the ground at one moment, and **carrying capacity** is what the forage will feed across a season. Growth, utilization, and weather all move one without moving the other, which is why the A1–A2 figures above are a range rather than a rate.

Establishment is the cost that catches people out. Measured per activity, native and pollinator-friendly covers run *below* turfgrass, and yet total vegetation O&M came out slightly *higher*, because the first three to five years take more separate passes across the site [@mccall2023]. Restorative ground cover is expensive to establish and competitive once established, so anyone arguing for it on cost savings alone should expect to meet an operator holding the establishment invoices.

So “solar grazing” on its own names three different practices, and which one a person means is usually settled by the size of the project they last worked on.
::::

::: {.caution}
**Citation caution.** The figures in the table above are widely misquoted with the activity labels transposed, reporting the mowing cost incurred *at* grazing sites as the cost *of* grazing. @stewart2025 give McCall's $279/ha/yr (= $113/acre/yr) as "the median cost for sheep grazing," where in McCall's Table 4 it is the median *mowing* cost at sheep-grazed sites; grazing itself ran about $50/acre/yr. Go to @mccall2023 directly.
:::

## Scale constrains design leverage {#sec-siting-latitude}

Every one of the six [design levers](design-levers.qmd) is available at every size. None of them holds the same range throughout, and the pattern is not a general loss of freedom as projects grow: three levers narrow or widen against each other, and two barely move at all.

**Siting latitude** is the freedom to choose where the array goes, and it is the lever the transect treats most sharply. What governs it changes as projects get bigger.

| Zone | What decides where it goes | Who actually chooses |
|---|---|---|
| **A1** | The yard, the herd, and the existing service drop | The operator, with almost no ground to choose among |
| **A2** | Spare corners, awkward field ends, ground already sitting idle | The operator |
| **A3** | Consistently low-yielding ground, where the water runs, buffer geometry | Developer and landowner, deliberately, together |
| **A4–A5** | Contiguous acreage near a substation and a place in the queue, nudged at the edges by prime-farmland rules, likely opposition, and which communities benefit | The land market and the grid, filtered through policy veto points |

**Structure** runs the opposite way and peaks where siting is weakest. At the farmstead an array is built to fit a particular yard, at a clearance the herd needs, out of whatever the local installer can source, because nothing about it has to be repeatable. Through the field and parcel zones the geometry answers to a crop. By A4 and A5 racking is a commodity bought by the megawatt, and the structural decision that still matters most is how much earth the system obliges anyone to move.

**Management** barely exists at A1, where the work is done by hand alongside the rest of the farm, and carries everything at A4 and A5, where seeding and grazing are contracted enterprises with their own line in the budget. That is the first crossing: siting and management trade places at A3.

![What scale leaves of each lever, in two registers. **On ground:** siting is opportunistic at the farmstead, widest in the middle, and taken away at A5 by land assembly and the interconnection queue; structure runs the other way, widest where an array can be built for one particular yard and narrowest where racking is bought by the megawatt; and management arrives only once a project is large enough to pay somebody to seed and graze it. Siting and management cross at A3. **On paper:** ownership and contracts trade against each other and cross at A3 as well, so one vertical carries both hand-offs. Ownership does restorative work for nothing at the small end, because the operator owns both the array and what stands under it, and none at all once the owner is absentee. Contracts are close to empty at A1, since there is no counterparty, and are the only lever with real reach left by A5. Scale is the axis, so it has no curve of its own.](../figures/fig_siting_latitude.svg){#fig-siting-latitude}

**Ownership and contracts run against each other**, which is why the figure gives them a panel of their own. Ownership does restorative work directly at the small end and stops doing it at the large end: an owner-operator needs no agreement, because the party deciding and the party living with the decision are the same person, and by A4 and A5 the owner is developer capital or a utility and the generation revenue has moved with them. Contracts run the opposite way. At A1 there is hardly a contract to write, since there is no counterparty; through A3 the instruments arrive, as a [PILOT](terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit), a subscription, a community-benefit agreement; and by A5 the lease is the only lever with real reach left. The alignment ownership supplies for nothing at the farmstead has to be manufactured, clause by clause, once the owner is somewhere else.

## Scale controls the dominant restoration mode {#sec-restoration-modes}

Leverage is about what is available. The [restoration mode](design-levers.qmd#sec-lv-mode) is about what actually did the work, and because the levers wax and wane against each other, the mode changes predictably along the transect. At A1 the operator controls the hardware and has almost no ground to choose among, so the work is **structure-led**. Through A2 and A3 latitude opens and placement becomes the strongest instrument available, so it is **siting-led**. By A4 and A5 the ground has been chosen by the land market and the queue, and restoration is carried by what grows and how it is run, so it is **management-led**.

At utility scale, restorative practice is mainly ground cover and grazing; at small and mid scale it is mainly placement [@macknick2022; @boggis2020]. That is why siting-led forms such as [solar prairie strips](archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) and [marginal land solar](archetypes.qmd#arch-marginal) live in the middle zones, and why a design that worked at A3 because of where it sat will not transfer to an A5 project however carefully the rest is copied.

**Restoration does not fall away with scale. It changes tool.** That is the useful thing to take from the crossing, and it is the reason the transect is worth naming at all: a developer told that restoration belongs to small projects has been given the wrong lever rather than the wrong ambition. The paper pair runs its own hand-off, and it falls in the same place. **Both crossings sit at A3**, which is the strongest thing the transect has to say about that zone: below it a project restores by choosing its ground and by who holds it, and above it by how the place is run and by what the parties signed. A3 is the one zone where all four are live at once, which is a stronger claim than A3 merely having the widest siting latitude. **Ownership-led** restoration is free at the farmstead and gone by A5, and **contract-led** restoration is nearly empty at A1 and the main instrument at A5. Between them the two cover the whole transect, which is why a utility-scale project is not out of restorative options: it has run out of the cheap ones.

## A3 has the most room to design {#sec-community-scale}

A3 sits at both crossings in @fig-siting-latitude, and it is the only zone where every restorative instrument is live at once. A parcel of forty or eighty acres is big enough that management arrives: someone is hired to seed it, a grazier turns up with a flock, and maintenance has a line of its own in the budget. It is also still small enough to place deliberately, because a developer and a landowner can walk the ground together and decide which part of it the array takes. At A1 there is almost nothing to choose among, and by A5 the choice has already been made by whatever acreage could be assembled near a substation. A typical US crop field runs fifty to ninety acres, so an A3 array fits inside one or two of them, which means it also fits inside one owner's decision.

**The stated assumption behind the ceiling.** A3 tops out at 5 MW because of an assumption about how much of a parcel restorative practice can take, and the assumption should be visible rather than buried in a capacity band. Take it that a restorative parcel array occupies **at most about a third of its parcel**, leaving the rest in production or in cover. On the 40 to 80 acre field that is typical of the US Midwest, a third is 12 to 24 acres. At the land intensities Berkeley Lab measures empirically for systems under 20 MW, 5.5 acres per MW-AC for fixed tilt and 6.3 for single-axis tracking, that is roughly **2 to 4 MW**, and about half that again for a wide-row agrivoltaic layout. Run it backwards and a 10 MW array needs some 63 acres of panel, which at a third of a parcel implies a 210 acre parcel: a farm rather than a field. So the zone stops where the arithmetic stops.

That the number lands near 5 MW is not only this document's arithmetic. Massachusetts caps SMART at 5 MW-AC per parcel, Minnesota, New York, and Maryland all cap community solar at 5 MW, California fast-tracks under 3 MW, Berkeley Lab splits its two national datasets at 5 MW-AC, and RMI puts community-scale solar at 0.5 to 5 MW. Policy, the data infrastructure, and the land arithmetic arrive at the same boundary from three directions. **The one-third assumption is the load-bearing one, and it has not been tested** (§-@sec-open-issues, issue 1): at half a parcel the same fields carry 3 to 7 MW and the case for a higher ceiling partly returns.

It also has a limit that is worth stating, because it is easy to over-apply. The assumption is about ground *taken*, so it governs the positions where production stops, [S3 through S5](sharing-sparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions). It does not govern [full sharing](sharing-sparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) (S1) at all, where coverage is not removal. An array spanning a vineyard covers the whole parcel and takes none of it, so the capacity that fits is set by row geometry rather than by any fraction of the field. Twenty acres of vines on eight-foot rows, with a single-axis tracker over every third row, carries something near 4.5 MW-AC while every row stays in production. Ground coverage and ground loss are different quantities, and only the second is what the third is a third of.

The band is more often called **community-scale solar**, and the phrase carries at least four senses worth separating. It means solar sized to a *community's* load rather than a wholesale market. It means solar sited where communities already are, on the distribution grid rather than on transmission. It means solar whose benefits are structured to reach a community, through subscription, tax base, or local ownership. And it means solar that builds community resilience, since a distribution-connected fleet fails differently than a single large plant. The Rocky Mountain Institute defines the class at 0.5 to 5 MW and calls it a sweet spot between utility-scale and behind-the-meter solar, on the grounds of economies of scale and distributed benefit. The restorative case for it is a different argument, and it is the one this document makes.

**The capacity is not a rounding error.** NREL's assessment of community solar technical potential, for systems from 38 kW to 67 MW, finds 967 GW-AC and 1,710 TWh a year under conservative siting assumptions, and 2,862 GW-AC under its reference case. The conservative figure alone is about sixty percent of the 1,600 GW-AC that DOE's Solar Futures Study puts at 2050 need [@ardani2021]. Per megawatt the middle is also not wasteful of land: NREL's land-use survey found plants between 1 and 20 MW used less direct area per megawatt than plants above 20 MW, 5.9 acres against 7.2. There is a measurement artifact worth knowing here, which is that conventional utility-scale potential studies apply a contiguity filter equivalent to omitting sites of 1.2 MW-AC or smaller, so much of this band is invisible by construction in the headline national numbers.

**What binds at A3 is money, not land.** Projects between 5 and 20 MW came in at \$2.19 per watt-AC in 2024 against \$1.38 above 250 MW, a penalty of about thirty-seven percent, because the paperwork does not scale down: a 2 MW project needs much the same letter of intent, EPC agreement, and power purchase agreement as a 200 MW one, and its offtaker is more likely to lack a credit rating. Some of the trade press calls this the messy middle, though the phrase is unstable and is used more often for the transition period in freight decarbonization than for a size class. The lexicon's own reading is that the zone with the most design freedom has the least access to capital, which is a reason A3 is under-built relative to what it could do rather than evidence that it should not be built.

::: {.caution}
**A prime-farmland claim that needs unpacking.** Studies that score solar facilities against soil quality find distribution-scale projects disproportionately on good land, and it is tempting to read that as careless siting. Two things complicate it.

The first is a confound. Community-scale solar goes where the load is, the load is where the people are, and the people are where the good soil was, because settlement followed arable land. Metropolitan areas hold a disproportionate share of the nation's prime farmland for that reason, and development pressure has concentrated on the best soils for a century [@dillman1982]. A fleet sited near load will sit on prime soil whether or not anyone was careless.

The second is resolution. A parcel classed as prime farmland is not uniformly productive. Across 338 US Midwest fields and 1,625 yield maps, about half of field area was high and stable, **32% was persistently low-yielding**, and 18% swung with the weather, with the unstable ground concentrated in wet depressions [@maestrini2018]. Roughly a third of a prime field, in other words, never performs. That 32% is exactly what siting latitude at A3 acts on, and a study that scores a facility by the soil class of its parcel cannot see whether the array took the good part or the bad part. The claim that mid-scale projects site carelessly and the claim that they site well are, at present, both untested at the resolution that would settle them.
:::

**Where the restoration lands is a matter of geometry.** The pollinator evidence comes from arrays in this band. Two Minnesota sites, 4.0 MW on 14 hectares and 5.5 MW on 17 hectares, produced bee visitation to soybean fifteen meters outside the fence at roughly two and a half times the rate inside the crop, with the effect bounded at half a kilometre to a kilometre and a half [@walston2018; @walston2024]. A [benefit delivered at that range](terminology.qmd#term-benefit-delivery) scales with perimeter and proximity rather than with area, which is a mechanical argument for many mid-sized arrays over a few large ones, and the ecological literature has posed that question without answering it: Tölgyesi and colleagues import the single-large-or-several-small debate from conservation biology and list guidance on park size as an open gap [@tolgyesi2023].

::: {.evidence}
**Evidence status.** Thin, and thinner than the confidence with which the middle is usually discussed. The capacity arithmetic is solid and federal. The delivery mechanism for pollination is measured, at two sites, for one function. Everything else is inference. Nobody has run the several-small-versus-one-large comparison at matched capacity and management, nobody has regressed land quality on project capacity at sub-parcel resolution, and no evaluation exists of whether the agricultural and pollinator adders in state incentive programs changed what actually got built. The [SCALE footprint](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale) is under-evidenced at every zone on this transect, not only here. Treat this section as an argument about where the decision still sits rather than a finding about where restoration has already happened.
:::
